## Big Idea

A good way to think about a tree ring is that it is the sum of several factors that govern growth. For example, the tree's diameter and age, the weather that year, something like a disturbance to the tree or what happened to its neighbors. And there is always  noise we can't account for. You never see those parts separately. If the answer to a math problem is 10 you don't know if that's from 3+2+4+1=10 or from 1+4+6-1=10, right?

One answer, a ring in this imagining, can't be taken apart into its constituent parts. But what if you had thousands of answers, and some of the terms turned up in more than one of them? Then you could start solving for the terms. That is kind of what a collection of cores is. Two cores from the same tree share its age trend and anything that happened to it (disturbance or competition for instance). Every tree in the stand shares the weather but different trees might be influenced by topography even if they are  close neighbors. Generally, the noisiest stuff is in each core alone. We use sampling design to try and get the most information we can in terms of pulling apart the different terms using different methods. 

In this chapter we are going to explore these different parts using a (deceptively) simple additive model of tree growth where we [explain the model here]

[once we have the model we can make a simulation of many cores and many trees]

By the end of the chapter you will know the parts of a ring width and what each method in the book is after and what it can be fooled by.

## How Fast It Changes

- New section, the second sort. The age trend and competition change over decades. Climate and noise change from year to year, with a year or two of memory. Disturbances arrive in one year and fade over years (the stand event) to decades (the release). Use the SIM10A figure again, reading it for speed this time.
- A small table, parts by who shares them and how fast they change. This is the table every method in the book can be placed on.
- A filter is the tool for sorting by speed, and the [aside that follows](03xAsideFiltering.qmd) takes it up. One or two sentences only.

## What Each Method Is After

- Rebuild the old closing table (method, part it is after, what it can mistake for that part, where in the book) as the center of the chapter, placed on the who-shares and how-fast table:
  - Crossdating keeps what is shared and fast. In raw widths the age trend looks shared (every tree slopes downhill), which is why the dating tools filter first.
  - Detrending removes what belongs to one tree and changes slowly, so it can take competition with the age trend, or a slow swing in climate.
  - A chronology keeps what is shared, so it can't tell climate from a stand-wide disturbance.
  - A tree series (`treeMean`) keeps what belongs to one tree, which is where a release shows.
- One worked example, the stand event of 1880, because it shows the model's limit in a single figure: a chronology can't tell $D2_t$ from $C_t$ without knowing which trees were hit. Keep the two-panel figure (or panel A only), the Douglass condition (many trees, a wide area, a long time), Cook's three hemlocks, and Wigley et al. and Buras on EPS. Decide in the draft whether the 1870s spline lift stays here or goes to [Detrending](09Detrending.qmd), which already calls it "chapter 2's puzzle".
- Keep Cook's "one researcher's 'signal' will frequently be another researcher's 'noise'" [@Cook1987, p. 38], and the climate and ecology views of the same parts. A record is good for a purpose.
